title: Mothers of the believers
hook: the Prophet's wives are called mothers of the believers (33:6)

segments.voice: Yesterday: uswah, the beautiful example, found in a trench. Your line was do the hard thing with them.

Khadijah. 'A'isha. Hafsah. Umm Salamah. Names you'll hear in Muslim families, called across playgrounds and written on school forms. In Muslim books, each is usually followed by a short phrase of honor: may God be pleased with her. Behind each name is a woman with her own story. And the Qur'an itself gives them, together, a title that turns a household into a family for a whole community. It's in Surah Al-Ahzab.

Pickthall: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their selves, and his wives are (as) their mothers." Ummahat al-mu'minin: the mothers of the believers. The title meant honor and respect. It also meant, as the surah says later, that no one could marry them after the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Who were they? The biographies list the women married to him at different times. Khadijah first, a widow and a merchant, remembered by tradition as the first to believe in his message; a report in Sahih Muslim says he married no one else while she lived. Sawdah, a widow who had emigrated to Abyssinia. 'A'isha, daughter of Abu Bakr, a great teacher of the early community; a large share of the hadith come through her. Hafsah, daughter of 'Umar, with whom the first gathered written pages of the Qur'an were kept. Zaynab bint Khuzaymah, called the mother of the poor for her charity. Umm Salamah, whose advice at Hudaybiyyah helped calm a crisis. Zaynab bint Jahsh, known for working with her hands and giving the money away. Juwayriyah, Umm Habibah, Safiyyah and Maymunah. Many were widows. Several came from families or tribes that had been at war with the Muslims. Biographers describe some marriages as alliances, some as acts of protection, and some as matches of affection. Sunni and Shia Muslims both use the title, and both honor Khadijah deeply; they differ in how they view some of the wives' roles in the conflicts after the Prophet's death. What the verse gives is a family: every believer, it says, has these mothers.

Khadijah, the first to believe; 'A'isha, the teacher; Hafsah, who kept the pages; Zaynab, mother of the poor; Umm Salamah, the adviser. Say her name slowly, think of what she might teach someone living now, and if you pray, ask God to be pleased with her.

chat.says: Why do Muslims call the Prophet's wives 'mothers of the believers'?
options: A Qur'an verse gives them that title, as an honor for the whole community.
Because each of them had children who became leaders of the early Muslims.
It's a later nickname from the biographies, not something the Qur'an says.
chat.meaning: Al-Ahzab 33:6 says his wives are as their mothers: a title of honor and respect that makes every believer their family.

Khadijah.meaning: the Prophet's first wife, remembered as the first to believe

Hafsah.meaning: daughter of 'Umar; the gathered Qur'an pages were kept with her

Abyssinia.meaning: an old name for the land of Ethiopia

Hudaybiyyah.meaning: a place near Mecca; site of a crisis Umm Salamah helped calm
